name: EPIC 220674823 b
significanceText: An ultra-short-period super-Earth that completes an orbit in just 14 hours, part of a rare class of planets found so close to their star that their formation and survival still puzzle astronomers.

name: HAT-P-7 b
significanceText: One of the first hot Jupiters found on a retrograde orbit, spinning backward relative to its star's rotation — a discovery that helped overturn the assumption that all planets orbit the same way their star spins.

name: HD 80653 b
significanceText: A rocky super-Earth so close to its star that a year lasts under 17 hours, with a bulk density consistent with iron and rock and no atmosphere left to speak of — a stripped-down world baking under extreme starlight.

name: K2-157 b
significanceText: A terrestrial planet whipping around its star in under 10 hours, sitting in a sparsely populated size-and-temperature zone nicknamed the "Neptunian savanna" between short-period rocky worlds and puffier Neptune-like planets.

name: KELT-16 b
significanceText: An inflated hot Jupiter orbiting so close to its star that it sits at just 1.7 Roche radii from being ripped apart, giving it a predicted lifespan of only a few hundred thousand years before tidal forces destroy it.

name: KELT-9 b
significanceText: The hottest giant planet ever found, with a dayside so scorching that molecules like water and methane can't hold together — its star is hot enough that the planet is being slowly evaporated by its own atmosphere's escape.

name: MASCARA-1 b
significanceText: The first planet discovered by the Multi-site All-Sky CAmeRA survey, this hot Jupiter circles a rapidly spinning, bright A-type star in a misaligned orbit and reflects starlight unusually well for a planet this hot.

name: TOI-1295 b
significanceText: A hot gas giant orbiting an F-type star every three days, adding to the growing catalog of close-in giants TESS has found around hotter, brighter stars than Kepler typically surveyed.

name: TOI-1431 b
significanceText: An inflated ultra-hot Jupiter orbiting one of the hottest and brightest stars known to host a planet, with a nightside almost as blazing as its dayside — a rare case where even the "cool" side of a planet glows.

name: TOI-1518 b
significanceText: An inflated ultra-hot Jupiter squeezed into a 1.9-day orbit around a bright, hot A/F-type star, offering astronomers a bright, easy target for probing atmospheric chemistry at extreme temperatures.

name: TOI-2109 b
significanceText: The shortest-period gas giant ever found, completing a full orbit in just 16 hours and running so hot that astronomers expect it to eventually spiral into its star — a planet quite literally living on borrowed time.

name: TOI-2260 b
significanceText: A super-Earth locked into a blistering 10-hour orbit around its star, part of the small and strange population of ultra-short-period rocky planets that shouldn't, by most formation models, have survived this close in.

name: TOI-2580 b
significanceText: A hot gas giant on a 3.4-day orbit around an F-type star, one of many close-in giants TESS has flagged for follow-up study of atmospheric composition and possible ongoing atmospheric escape.

name: WASP-103 b
significanceText: The first exoplanet directly measured to be squashed into a slightly oval, rugby-ball shape by its star's gravity — a real-world confirmation of the tidal deformation theorists had long predicted for planets this close in.

name: WASP-121 b
significanceText: Nicknamed Tylos, this ultra-hot Jupiter was the first planet found losing heavy metals like magnesium and iron straight out of its atmosphere, and the first shown to have a genuine stratosphere — a layer that heats up with altitude, just like Earth's.

name: WASP-167 b
significanceText: A hot Jupiter on a backward, retrograde orbit around a rapidly rotating, pulsating star, discovered jointly by two separate survey teams and confirmed by mapping the planet's shadow across the star's spinning face rather than by standard velocity measurements.

name: WASP-178 b
significanceText: An ultra-hot Jupiter orbiting the second-hottest star known to host any planet, second only to KELT-9 — its atmosphere shows signs of iron and magnesium and lacks the strong day-night winds seen on similar worlds.

name: WASP-18 b
significanceText: A gas giant ten times Jupiter's mass squeezed into a less-than-one-day orbit, exerting tidal forces so strong they may be distorting its own star's internal structure and aging it prematurely.

name: WASP-33 b
significanceText: The first exoplanet ever found orbiting a pulsating star, circling its rapidly spinning host on a retrograde, tilted orbit that made this delta Scuti-type variable the first known exoplanet host of its kind.

name: Wendelstein-2 b
significanceText: A hot Jupiter discovered through a citizen-science-supported survey out of the Wendelstein Observatory, part of a hunt for close-in giant planets around cooler, less-studied K-type stars where such planets are rarer than around Sun-like stars.
